8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":20,"verseId":10,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Cause and Effect (Saṃbhava)","totalVerses":24,"verseData":{"id":"v20_10","number":10,"title":"Summary Dilemma: Ceased Causes Can't Produce, Persisting Causes Can't Either","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"How can a cause, having ceased and dissolved, Give rise to a produced effect? How can a cause joined with its effect produce it If they persist together?"},"philosophy":{"insight":"A summary verse recapitulating the temporal dilemma: (1) If the cause has CEASED — how can something that no longer exists produce anything? (2) If the cause PERSISTS alongside the effect — how can a co-existing thing \"produce\" its companion? Neither cessation nor persistence enables inherent production.","madhyamaka":"Hetu niruddha vinaṣṭa katham phala utpādayet (how can a ceased, dissolved cause produce an effect?). Hetu phala-saṃyukta tiṣṭhamāna katham utpādayet (how can a cause persisting joined with the effect produce it?). Both horns fail: ceased causes can't act; persisting causes can't produce co-existents.","quantum":"Quantum decoherence: the quantum state \"ceases\" (decoheres) during measurement, yet produces a classical outcome. How? Not through inherent production but through a conventional process. Like v.10: neither inherent cessation nor inherent persistence explains production. Conventional process does.","bridge":"Both quantum decoherence and v.10 face the \"how does production work?\" question. QM: the quantum state decoheres (ceases) but produces outcomes — conventionally, not inherently. V.10: ceased causes can't produce, persisting causes can't either. Both: production is a conventional process, not an inherent mechanism.","accessible":"Two impossible scenarios: (1) The chef is gone — who cooks the meal? (2) The chef and the meal already exist together — what's left to cook? Neither absence nor co-presence of the chef makes sense for inherent cooking. Conventional cooking works because it's a process, not an inherent event.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: causes cease and effects arise in sequence — this process works. Ultimately: neither the cessation nor the persistence is inherent. The process is conventional, and it works precisely because it's empty.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying production doesn't happen. Conventional production works perfectly. The verse shows that INHERENT production is inexplicable — whether the cause ceases or persists. Convention works; inherence doesn't."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Decoherence — Conventional Process Beyond Inherent Mechanism","score":55,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Decoherence: the quantum state \"ceases\" (loses coherence) while producing classical outcomes — not through inherent mechanism but conventional process. V.10: neither ceased nor persisting causes can inherently produce. Both: production is processual, not mechanistic.","caveat":"Decoherence is a physics process. V.10 is a philosophical dilemma. The parallel is about production as process, not as inherent mechanism."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"Two scenarios side by side: (1) A dissolved cause with a question mark — \"How can it produce?\" (2) A cause and effect sitting together — \"What needs to be produced?\" Neither scenario enables production. Caption: \"Inherent production fails either way.\"","educationalGoal":"User sees the complete temporal dilemma: ceased → can't act; persisting → can't produce. Neither works for inherent causation."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why is this verse a summary?","a":"It distills the arguments of vv.5-9 into a single, clear dilemma: (1) Ceased cause → can't produce (vv.6, 9). (2) Persisting cause → can't produce (vv.5, 7). The summary reinforces the temporal section's conclusion by presenting both horns together.","realLifeExample":"A lawyer's closing argument: \"Either the defendant was absent (and couldn't have done it) or was present (and had no motive). Either way: not guilty of inherent production.\""},{"q":"Why can't a ceased cause produce?","a":"Something that no longer exists can't DO anything — including producing effects. A ceased cause has no causal power left. This is the annihilationist horn: complete cessation = complete powerlessness.","realLifeExample":"A dead battery can't power a phone. If the cause is \"dead\" (ceased), it can't power (produce) the effect."},{"q":"Why can't a persisting cause produce?","a":"If the cause and effect co-exist simultaneously, the effect is already there — what needs to be produced? \"Production\" implies bringing something new into existence. If it's already there (co-existing), production hasn't occurred.","realLifeExample":"If you and the cake are both in the kitchen already, there's nothing to \"bake.\" The cake is already present. Production requires the effect to NOT already exist alongside the cause."},{"q":"How does this connect to the spatial analysis?","a":"Spatial (vv.1-4): effect in/not-in cause. Temporal (vv.5-10): cause ceased/persisting. BOTH dimensions yield the same dilemma structure: both options fail for inherent production. The analysis is remarkably parallel across space and time.","realLifeExample":"Two inspections of a building: (1) structural (spatial) — both options fail. (2) Historical (temporal) — both options fail. Same building, same conclusion, different angles."},{"q":"What is the significance of the \"dissolved\" (vinaṣṭa) language?","a":"\"Dissolved\" emphasizes the COMPLETENESS of inherent cessation: not just changing form but completely vanishing. This strengthens the argument: even if \"ceased\" might admit some residual, \"dissolved\" allows none. From nothing, nothing arises.","realLifeExample":"The difference between \"the company closed\" (might have assets remaining) and \"the company dissolved\" (legally nothing remains). V.10 uses the stronger \"dissolved\" to close every loophole."},{"q":"What comes after this summary?","a":"V.11 will address the necessity of connection between cause and effect. VV.12-14 will examine simultaneity across all temporal combinations. V.15 will state the final dilemma of connection/non-connection.","deeper":"V.10 is strategically placed as a summary of the temporal section before moving to the connectional section (vv.11-15). By summarizing the temporal dilemma in one clear verse, Nāgārjuna prepares the ground for a new angle of attack: not WHEN the cause relates to the effect but HOW they're connected. The move from temporal to connectional analysis reflects the systematic architecture of Ch.20: spatial → temporal → connectional → essential → conclusion."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What is the dilemma of v.10?","options":["A) Only one option","B) (1) Ceased cause can't produce — it's gone.
